query: Earlier studies used carbothermal shock, fast moving-bed pyrolysis, microwave heating, polyol synthesis, and dealloying, but a straightforward, cost-effective, and scalable route remains unavailable. Prior comparative work produced sharply different outcomes among multimetal nanoparticle systems—including homogeneous alloy formation versus phase separation, elemental segregation, uncontrolled morphology, and high decomposition temperatures—without establishing a general cause. The challenge increases with more than five interacting elements and the requirement to preserve substantial surface-atom exposure for catalytic applications. Against this background, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles and why? Describe one controlled comparison without naming the variable or investigative technique, predict the observations relative to an unchanged baseline, define where the hypothesis should and should not apply, relate it to the reported comparative evidence, and identify a decisive falsifying result.

generation.hypothesis: Noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles form successfully when a support surface facilitates a rapid, synchronized reduction of all metal precursors by generating high-potential reduction species that mediate simultaneous nucleation, thereby overcoming differences in individual reduction kinetics and preventing phase segregation.
generation.material_initial_state: A uniformly dispersed mixture of noble and base metal precursors deposited on a metal oxide support that is capable of activating reduction species (e.g., via known spillover effects).
generation.intervention: Modify the support to enhance its capability to generate and transport reduction species during precursor reduction, compared to an otherwise identical support lacking these properties.
generation.conditions: Synthesis performed under low-temperature conditions that allow for the reduction of metal salts without promoting extensive atomic diffusion; the metal precursor molar ratios and dispersion on the support remain constant across tests.
generation.structural_mediator: Surface-bound, highly reducing species (e.g., hydrogen species generated at noble metal sites on the support) that migrate across the interface to rapidly reduce neighboring precursors.
generation.mechanism: Reduction initiated at noble metal sites on the support generates spillover species that quickly migrate to adjacent base metal precursors. This rapid, support-mediated simultaneous reduction leads to co-nucleation of all metal atoms, promoting a homogeneously alloyed nanoparticle rather than a phase‐segregated or intermetallic structure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under enhanced support conditions, nanoparticles will exhibit a uniformly mixed, single-phase HEA structure with substantial surface atom exposure. In contrast, the baseline (i.e., when the support is not modified for enhanced reduction mediation) will yield nanoparticles with signs of phase separation or elemental segregation.
generation.baseline: Synthesis of an identical mixture on a support lacking the enhanced reduction mediation property, expected to show less synchronous reduction and a higher likelihood of phase separation or uncontrolled morphologies.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to apply to precursor systems where at least one component (typically a noble metal) can generate the reducing species necessary for spillover effects, and under synthesis conditions that do not impart excessive thermal energy leading to thermodynamic equilibration. It may not be applicable to unsupported powders or systems where the disparity in intrinsic reduction potentials is too great to be overcome by the support effect.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of the spillover effect and the precise threshold of support modification needed to achieve synchrony remain uncertain; additionally, the role of precursor coordination environments may further complicate the reduction kinetics.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two experimental sets using an identical noble and base metal precursor mixture deposited on two supports: one with an enhanced capability for generating and transporting reduction species (via a known modification that promotes spillover) and one without this modification. Monitor the reduction and nanoparticle formation process in situ under identical low-temperature conditions.
measurements: In situ XANES to follow the reduction states of noble and base metals simultaneously
XRD to determine crystal phase formation
TEM/EDS to assess elemental homogeneity and morphology of nanoparticles
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both sets yield nanoparticles with indistinguishable phase composition, elemental distributions, and morphologies, then the tested support-mediated synchronous reduction mechanism would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Our own group has previously demonstrated that TiO2 is a promising platform for the synthesis of non-equilibrium binary alloy NPs, such as RuNi and RhCu, which are essentially immiscible at equilibrium due to the positive enthalpies of formation of their solid solution alloys,. However, the highly specific formation of binary alloy NPs based on combinations of normally immiscible noble and base metals can be achieved with the assistance of the strong spillover effect obtained from TiO2. Using this oxide allows spillover hydrogen species with high reduction potentials to be generated from noble metals (Ru or Rh) and to rapidly migrate to and reduce base metals (Ni or Cu) at low temperatures. In the present work, we developed and demonstrated that this facile strategy can be applied to the synthesis of TiO2-supported HEA NPs. Specifically, CoNiCuRuPd HEA NPs on TiO2 displayed high activity and outstanding stability during the CO2 hydrogenation reaction. This study also elucidated the specific mechanism responsible for the formation of HEA NPs, based on in situ characterization techniques.
